# 1 Enoch Chapter 6 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

This log records all verses in 1 Enoch Chapter 6 where the three translators (EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA) significantly diverged in their renderings, along with SOPHIA's resolution and reasoning.

---

## 6:2 — 'lusted after' vs. 'desired' vs. 'burned with desire' for Ge'ez sexual attraction

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "lusted after" | Strong verb preserves the transgressive nature of angelic desire for humans |
| LOGOS | "desired" | Neutral verb; lets context convey the transgression |
| PNEUMA | "burned with desire" | Intensified idiom capturing the consuming nature of the attraction |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted 'desired' (LOGOS). The Ge'ez verb is not inherently pejorative — it is the same verb used for normal desire. The transgression lies in the agents (angels) and objects (humans), not in the verb itself. EMET's 'lusted' and PNEUMA's 'burned' both import moral judgment into the lexeme.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS. Semantically significant — the verb itself is neutral.

---

## 6:6 — 'Hermon' etymology — whether to gloss the wordplay on herem (oath/curse)

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "they-called it Mount Hermon, because they-had-sworn" | Preserves the Ge'ez etymology linking Hermon to the oath |
| LOGOS | "they called it Mount Hermon, because they had sworn and bound themselves by mutual curses upon it" | Full clause preserving the etymological explanation |
| PNEUMA | "they named it Hermon because that is where they swore their oath" | Cleaner English; makes the etymology explicit |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS rendering. The wordplay on Hermon/herem (ban, oath, curse) is central to the chapter's theology — the mountain of God's holiness becomes the mountain of angelic rebellion. All three preserve it; LOGOS gives the fullest form.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS. Etymological — preserves a key theological wordplay.

---
